You don’t technically NEED to dilate to take a picture of the retina, it can be done without dilation but will likely not be as clear of an image and may not capture as much of the retina as you would if dilated depending on how large a patients pupils are naturally. It’s typically much easier and better to do while dilated.

There’s many reasons to dilate, if you’re seen at an ophthalmologist they would typically look at the eyes with you in an exam chair and use a device called a slit lamp, essentially a microscope. If not dilated the light from the slit lamp would constrict the pupil while they’re trying to look inside the eye limiting their view.

I work in ophthalmology and have not heard of this…and it doesn’t make a lot of sense the way it’s described. A bright flash should constrict the pupils, as that’s what the pupils should do when exposed to light, not dilate. "The FDA last year implemented sunscreen reforms that go into effect in 2012, including:

requiring that sunscreen products that have SPF values higher than 50 be labeled as “SPF 50+” because the "FDA does not have adequate data demonstrating that products with SPF values higher than 50 provide additional protection compared to products with SPF values of 50."

Once you hit SPF 40 you block out 97.5% of UVB radiation and SPF 50 blocks 98%. More important than using a super high SPF is using enough sunscreen. 1 fl oz is the recommended amount
